name: Colloids
kicker: Tiny particles spread through another substance · Milk, fog, and gelatin
briefing: A colloid is a mixture whose particles are much bigger than most molecules but still too small to see or to settle out, so they stay spread through another substance, as in milk, fog, whipped cream, and gelatin. Shine a flashlight through one and the beam lights up, because the particles scatter light, a trick called the Tyndall effect. Scottish chemist Thomas Graham named them in 1861 from the Greek word for “glue.”
answerHtml: Colloids (accept colloidal dispersions or colloidal suspensions; prompt on heterogeneous mixtures or dispersions; do not accept “suspension” or “solution” alone)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: Richard Zsigmondy [“ZHIG-mon-dee”] won the 1925 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for studying these mixtures, using an ultramicroscope he helped invent to see light scattered by their particles. That instrument let scientists count particles far too small for an ordinary microscope.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these mixtures, such as milk, fog, and gelatin, whose particles are too small to settle out but large enough to scatter light.

tossups.p: The Svedberg won the 1926 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for studying these mixtures, inventing the ultracentrifuge to make their tiny particles settle. Jean Perrin [“zhahn peh-RAN”] won the Physics Nobel the same year, partly for experiments on how particles in these mixtures settle and jiggle.
tossups.r: That jiggling is called Brownian motion. For 10 points, name these mixtures, like milk and fog, whose particles stay spread out instead of settling.

tossups.p: Thomas Graham, who also has a law about how fast gases effuse, named these mixtures in 1861 from the Greek word for “glue.” Graham used membranes to separate them from dissolved salts, a process called dialysis that he pioneered.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these mixtures, such as mayonnaise and whipped cream, which fall between solutions and suspensions in particle size.

tossups.p: Butter and milk are both emulsions, a kind of these mixtures, but butter holds water droplets in fat, while milk holds fat droplets in water. Adding salt can make the particles in many of these mixtures clump together, a process called flocculation or coagulation.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these mixtures, like fog and gelatin, whose particles scatter a beam of light in the Tyndall effect.

tossups.p: The Roman Lycurgus [“lye-KUR-gus”] Cup looks green in reflected light and red when lit from behind, because its glass is one of these mixtures, holding tiny particles of gold and silver. In 1857, Michael Faraday made a ruby-red example containing tiny gold particles.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these mixtures whose particles are too small to settle out, such as milk and fog.

tossups.p: River deltas form partly because fine clay particles spread through river water clump together when they meet salty seawater. Electrostatic precipitators clean smoke, one of these mixtures, out of factory chimneys by giving its tiny particles an electric charge and then collecting them on metal plates.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these mixtures whose particles, between about 1 and 1,000 nanometers across, scatter light in the Tyndall effect.

tossups.p: Because the particles in many of these mixtures carry electric charge, they drift toward an electrode in an electric field, a process called electrophoresis. Those particles usually all carry the same kind of charge, so they repel each other instead of clumping together.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these mixtures, which include emulsions, foams, and gels, whose particles never settle out.

tossups.p: Chemists sort these mixtures into lyophilic [“lye-oh-FIL-ik”] types, whose particles attract the liquid around them, and lyophobic types, whose particles do not. In water treatment, alum is added to make these mixtures of dirt particles clump and sink.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these mixtures, like milk, whose particles stay spread out instead of settling and make a flashlight beam visible.

tossups.p: Above a certain concentration, soap molecules gather into balls called micelles [“my-SELLZ”], forming “association” types of these mixtures. Egg yolk helps make mayonnaise one of these mixtures by keeping drops of oil spread through a watery liquid.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these mixtures, whose types include emulsions and aerosols, that scatter light in the Tyndall effect.

tossups.p: Some of these mixtures are thixotropic [“thik-suh-TROP-ik”], becoming runnier when they are shaken or stirred and thickening again at rest. In a gel, one type of these mixtures, a liquid is trapped inside a network of solid particles or strands.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these mixtures, including gelatin, whose particles are larger than those in solutions but smaller than those in suspensions.

tossups.p: No gas-in-gas type of these mixtures exists, because gases always mix evenly into a solution. Smoke is one of these mixtures with solid particles spread through a gas, while fog spreads liquid droplets through a gas, and both are called aerosols.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these mixtures, like milk and whipped cream, whose particles do not settle out over time.

tossups.p: The random jiggling of particles in these mixtures is named for botanist Robert Brown, who watched tiny bits from pollen grains doing it in water in 1827. Albert Einstein explained that jiggling in 1905 as the result of collisions with moving molecules.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these mixtures, such as fog and milk, that scatter light in the Tyndall effect.

tossups.p: NASA’s Stardust spacecraft caught comet dust in aerogel, a super-light solid made by drying one type of these mixtures. Marshmallows, pumice, and plastic foam cups are “solid foam” examples of these mixtures, with gas bubbles trapped in a solid.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these mixtures, which also include emulsions like milk and mayonnaise.

tossups.p: Unlike the particles in a suspension, the particles in these mixtures pass through ordinary filter paper, but much finer membranes can trap them. Milk is one of these mixtures called an emulsion, and homogenizing it breaks its butterfat into smaller droplets so the cream does not rise.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these mixtures, like fog and gelatin, that fall between solutions and suspensions in particle size.

tossups.p: Each of these mixtures has a dispersed phase spread through a continuous phase called the dispersion medium. Many paints and inks are sols, the type of these mixtures with solid particles in a liquid, while gelatin and jelly are gels.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these mixtures, like milk and fog, that scatter a beam of light in the Tyndall effect.

clues.t: A mixture with tiny particles spread through another substance that never settle out
Examples include milk, fog, whipped cream, mayonnaise, and gelatin
Their particles scatter a beam of light, like headlights in fog: the Tyndall effect
Their particles are bigger than those in a solution but smaller than those in a suspension
Particles are about 1 to 1,000 nanometers across
Made of a dispersed phase spread through a continuous phase called the dispersion medium
Emulsions are liquid in liquid, like milk and mayonnaise; in mayonnaise, egg yolk keeps oil drops spread through water
Foams are gas in liquid (whipped cream, shaving cream); solid foams are gas in solid (marshmallows, pumice)
Aerosols are liquid or solid particles in a gas: fog and clouds (liquid) and smoke (solid)
Gels trap a liquid in a solid network (gelatin, jelly); sols have solid particles in a liquid (many paints and inks)
No gas-in-gas type exists, because gases always mix evenly into a solution
Their particles jiggle randomly in Brownian motion, named for Robert Brown, who saw it in 1827
Named in 1861 by Thomas Graham, from the Greek word for “glue”
Their particles pass through ordinary filter paper but can be trapped by much finer membranes
Thomas Graham, of Graham’s law of effusion, pioneered dialysis, using membranes to separate them from dissolved salts
Richard Zsigmondy helped invent the ultramicroscope and won the 1925 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for studying them
1926 Nobels: The Svedberg (Chemistry; invented the ultracentrifuge) for studying them, and Jean Perrin (Physics) partly for experiments on how their particles settle
Albert Einstein explained Brownian motion in 1905 as the result of collisions with moving molecules
Butter holds water droplets in fat, while milk holds fat droplets in water; both are emulsions
Adding salt can make the particles clump together, called coagulation or flocculation
Electrostatic precipitators clean smoke from factory chimneys by charging its tiny particles and collecting them on metal plates
Alum clumps dirt particles in water treatment; river clay clumping in salty seawater helps form deltas
Their particles usually carry the same kind of charge, so they repel each other; in an electric field they drift toward an electrode (electrophoresis)
Lyophilic types have particles that attract the surrounding liquid; lyophobic types do not
Above a certain concentration, soap molecules form micelles, making “association” types
Thixotropic ones get runnier when shaken or stirred and thicken again at rest
Gold and silver particles make the Roman Lycurgus Cup look green or red; Michael Faraday made a ruby-red gold sample in 1857
NASA’s Stardust probe caught comet dust in aerogel, a super-light solid made by drying a gel

trap.title: Not solution or suspension
trap.body: These mixtures are defined by particle size, so tossups about them often describe solutions and suspensions too. In a solution, like salt water, the particles are single molecules or ions and a light beam passes through unseen; in a suspension, like muddy water, the particles are big enough to settle out or be filtered. Players also blurt one type, like “emulsion” or “aerosol,” when the question wants the whole family.
trap.fix: Settles out or filters out means suspension; perfectly clear with no visible beam means solution; scatters a beam (the Tyndall effect) but never settles means this answer. Listen for “these mixtures” and give the general name unless the question clearly asks for one type.
trap.line: Real answer line: Colloids (accept colloidal dispersions or colloidal suspensions; prompt on heterogeneous mixtures or dispersions; do not accept “suspension” or “solution” alone)
